question: Examine the continuity and differentiability of the function $f(x)=|x^2-4|$ at $x=2$, using the appropriate one-sided limits and one-sided derivatives, and justify your conclusion.
explanation:
Continuity at $x=2$
The value of the function at $x=2$ is $$f(2)=|2^2-4|=0.$$ For values of $x$ sufficiently close to $2$ with $x<2$, we have $x^2-4<0$, so $$f(x)=4-x^2.$$ Hence, $$\lim_{x\to2^-}f(x)=\lim_{x\to2^-}(4-x^2)=0.$$ For $x>2$, $x^2-4>0$, so $$f(x)=x^2-4.$$ Therefore, $$\lim_{x\to2^+}f(x)=\lim_{x\to2^+}(x^2-4)=0.$$ Thus, $$\lim_{x\to2^-}f(x)=\lim_{x\to2^+}f(x)=f(2)=0,$$ and hence $f$ is continuous at $x=2$.

Differentiability at $x=2$
For $x<2$ near $2$, $$f(x)=4-x^2,$$ so the left-hand derivative at $2$ is $$f'_-(2)=\left.\frac{d}{dx}(4-x^2)\right|_{x=2}=-2(2)=-4.$$ For $x>2$, $$f(x)=x^2-4,$$ so the right-hand derivative is $$f'_+(2)=\left.\frac{d}{dx}(x^2-4)\right|_{x=2}=2(2)=4.$$ Since $$f'_-(2)\neq f'_+(2),$$ the derivative of $f$ at $x=2$ does not exist.

Final Result
The function $f(x)=|x^2-4|$ is continuous at $x=2$ but is not differentiable at $x=2$.

options.B: $f$ is both continuous and differentiable at $x=2$.
options.C: $f$ is neither continuous nor differentiable at $x=2$.
options.D: $f$ is continuous but not differentiable at $x=2$, with $f'_-(2)=-4$ and $f'_+(2)=4$.
